title: SIXTH REPORT: Alpha School’s Survival Challenge — literally
author: Benjamin Riley
summary: Benjamin Riley continues his investigation of Alpha School, the AI-driven private school network, with three newly confirmed facts about its high school Survival Challenge at a Texas ranch. First, students were required to surrender their medical supplies, including epi-pens and inhalers, until the event ended. Second, attendance was not taken once the weekend began, despite a 250-acre site with minimal fencing. Third, he adds details about an adult guide who reported heat stroke, left to see a doctor and was fired soon afterward, while withholding the guide's name. He cites food allergy, asthma and Texas Education Agency sources to argue that these practices violate basic duties of care that apply to ordinary schools. His commentary concludes that the event put students' lives at risk and questions how any parent could feel safe about future Alpha trips, ending with the question of what it will take for action.
points: Confiscating epi-pens and inhalers for the whole weekend removed students' access to life-saving treatment, which the author argues has no justification under medical guidance.

Skipping attendance between the start and end of the event meant students on a large, lightly fenced ranch could have gone unaccounted for up to 48 hours, contrary to Texas guidance on student safety.
The firing of a guide who reported heat stroke and obtained a doctor's note is presented as a further sign of weak safety culture, though the author withholds the name for confidentiality.

The report relies on multiple confirming sources and explicit sourcing to state regulators and medical bodies, which is why it is useful as a record of accountability questions for AI-forward schools.
The commentary links the incident to the school's other trips, asking what parents are supposed to trust given these lapses.
quotes: Alpha School put its students’ lives in danger during the Survival Challenge by confiscating their medical supplies.
What is known that is some of the medical supplies that students were deprived of over the weekend included epi-pens and inhalers, according to multiple sources.

For three days and two nights, Alpha School students were deprived of access to their epi-pens. While the severity of students’ anaphylaxis conditions are unknown, there is no justification — none — for any policy or practice that results in students lacking access to this potentially life-saving medical device.

What I have since learned through multiple sources is that Alpha School did not take the attendance of students once the Survival Challenge commenced — students were accounted for at the beginning of the event and when it concluded, but not in between.

This is why so-called normal schools take attendance with regularity: at all times, public schools must be able to account for the whereabouts of the children in their care in order to keep them safe.

Sources indicate that other staff disagreed with this self-assessment. Sources further indicate this guide then left the ranch of their own volition to visit a hospital in Victoria, Texas, and obtained a note from a doctor that stated the guide should no longer stay on the ranch, and should instead return home.

I simply do not know how any parent could feel safe about their child’s participation in these trips, given the inexplicable confiscation of students’ medical supplies, and the failure to take regular attendance to monitor students’ whereabouts.
